en: The Elephant’s Armpit Sūtra, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmamitra of Jibin during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great [assembly].

There were five hundred bhikṣus together with sixty thousand bodhisattvas—renowned throughout the world, possessed of dhāraṇīs, possessing unhindered eloquence, teaching the Dharma without duality, and having accomplished inconceivable supernatural powers—their names being as follows:

The Bodhisattva Unfailing Resolve, the Bodhisattva Transcending Renown and Power-Treasury, the Bodhisattva Jewel-Moon Flower, the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Thunder-Lamp, the Bodhisattva Immeasurable Contemplation Emanating from All Worlds, the Bodhisattva Mountain Hero, the Bodhisattva Joyful Birth, the Bodhisattva Pure Arms Unobstructed Radiance, the Bodhisattva Understanding the Minds of Sentient Beings, the Bodhisattva Vajra-Achieved Firmness, the Bodhisattva Understanding the Speech of All Sentient Beings and Detachment, the Bodhisattva Brahma-Sound Heroic Power, the Bodhisattva Renowned Face Unobstructed Awakening, and the Bodhisattva Jewel-Cluster of All Roots of Virtue.
The youth Mañjuśrī was accompanied by sixty thousand bodhisattvas, headed by these foremost ones.
At that time, the venerable Śāriputra arose from meditative concentration in the late afternoon and approached the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat beneath a different tree and entered the samādhi of tranquility.

Then, the Venerable Śāriputra, seeing from afar the World-Honored One’s serene deportment, quickly took some grass, spread it out to form a seat, and sat cross-legged; while he sat with his body upright, [the Buddha emerged from meditation].
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, while still in his seat, had this thought: "How marvelous!

Such is the Tathāgata’s practice of tranquility, the root of peace and happiness, which brings peace and happiness to all sentient beings, and who also knows the samādhi of the nature of all phenomena."
At that time, the World-Honored One arose calmly from samādhi and made a sound of clearing his throat.
Hearing the Tathāgata’s sound of clearing his throat, Śāriputra experienced a joyous bliss and was moved by compassion; he immediately went to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he stood before the Buddha; after paying homage to the Buddha, he spoke these verses:

"If there are sentient beings who are free from discrimination, And who do not even form mental conceptions regarding phenomena, Entering samādhi while constantly moving through the world, They always endure and delight in such a Dharma."
Seeing no distinction among sentient beings, they are like those liberated through the nature of illusion;
discerning that all phenomena have the essence of space, they are free from the notion of self and experience peace and bliss.
Within the state of harmony, there is no thought of attachment;
there is no delusion regarding the perception of things, nor is there arising or non-arising. Such a one does not perceive a life-force, yet experiences peace and bliss.
Having no conceptualization regarding sentient beings, these sentient beings are not [truly] sentient beings;
being without sound regarding the marks of sentient beings, those who have no view of self are at peace.
Wisdom does not discriminate among sentient beings; this is the attainment of the dharma-realm free from contention.
One who discerns all perceptions of a "great man" is no different from an awakened one; such a person dwells in peace and bliss.
One should dwell well in generosity and the observance of precepts, always practicing clear comprehension free from the stain of stinginess;
abiding in the dharma that is undefiled, one sees that peace and bliss wherein there is no perception of high or low.
Those who have attained that patience are exceedingly courageous; they possess neither the dual views of hatred nor love.
They find neither diligence nor indolence; those free from conceptual thought are at peace.
Practicing meditative concentration with steadfastness, Nor even conceptualizing it as distraction—
One who thus well understands the dharma of meditative concentration, And is free from the notion of "meditation," dwells in peace and bliss.
Without conceptualization and without wisdom, yet not lacking wisdom to attain mastery;
neither clever nor foolish—those free from discursive thought are at peace.
Whether in the wilderness or in a village, he practices with equanimity in all places;
having no aversion toward the village and no pride in the wilderness, he dwells in peace and happiness.
Fully endowed with all requisites for alms-seeking, yet never harboring the thought of seeking alms,
nor ever conceiving the thought "I am seeking alms"— one who has no such thoughts of seeking is at peace.
If there are discarded robes from a refuse heap, one gathers them and wears them over the body;
yet, one has no thought of possessing these worn-out clothes, nor does one treat others with contempt—thus one dwells in peace and happiness.
Praised by the Sugata and permitted by the Buddha, one who properly receives and uses the three dharma robes,
free from the conceit "I am practicing rightly," and devoid of divergent thoughts, is at peace.
If the speaker of the Dharma is supreme and sublime, And there is neither self nor sentient being,
Nor even a mind that thinks, "I am preaching the Dharma," Then one who is unattached to the unreal dwells in peace and happiness.
Regarding all roots of goodness, they have no notion of reality; they have no notion of substantiality and no notion of craving.
Without conceptualizing or discriminating among the various fetters and afflictions, those who practice non-duality dwell in peace and happiness.
Having no notion of arising amidst what arises, and perceiving the defects of all dwelling places,
one who constantly exerts diligence day and night and is free from conceptual proliferation is at peace.
Nor does one dwell in false imaginings regarding what is not the proper place; nor does one discriminate with regard to superior wisdom.
There is no distinction between the Tathāgata and non-Buddhists; being free from arrogance, that is the sublime peace and bliss.
Immeasurable, innumerable, and limitless, never departing from that which is equal to space;
with no thought of distinction between myself and sentient beings, and seeing neither increase nor decrease, I behold their peace and bliss.

If one attains the practice even in dreams, and through eloquence transforms the ignorant, acting in the world like the moon in water—there is no further progress for such a one; they possess all happiness.
Through various skillful means, one realizes the ultimate truth; Without clinging to the notion of a solid self in birth and death, One awakens to the subtle and quiescent Dharma;
For those who practice without conceptualization, there is peace and bliss.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Śāriputra:
"Excellent, excellent!
Your profound wisdom and practice enable you to turn the wheel of Dharma."
"You, Śāriputra!
Command all the bhikṣus and bodhisattvas on this Vulture Peak Mountain who have entered meditative concentration to assemble!"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
I am not capable of this.”
"Why is this? For those such as these are all majestic and powerful great dragons.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a radiance from his body; the light he emitted shone everywhere throughout immeasurable and boundless Buddha-worlds, and all the bodhisattvas came to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Having arrived, they all remained suspended in mid-air.
These bhikṣus and bodhisattvas arose from their meditative absorption and proceeded to where the Buddha was.
From the city of Rājagṛha, immeasurable thousands of beings came to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the entire assembly had gathered, looked upon the face of the youth Mañjuśrī and smiled.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what cause and for what reason do you smile?
Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not smile without a cause.
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"In the past, within this Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, ten thousand Buddhas preached the *Gajapraśna Sūtra*.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had said, rose quickly from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
Excellent, Sugata!
You should now expound this *Hastikakṣya Sūtra*, for this sūtra is difficult to hear.
If the Tathāgata were to speak it, it would cause all doubts to vanish.
This profound and wondrous scripture possesses deep radiance.
World-Honored One,
for what reason did you smile after gazing upon the face of Mañjuśrī?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!”
"Discerning with wholesome wisdom,
Ānanda, listen now attentively,
listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!"
"I shall now speak.
After Ānanda had received the Buddha’s instruction, the Buddha said to Ānanda:

"If there are sentient beings who understand this sutra, they possess the strength of a great elephant and the strength of a great dragon; those sentient beings who understand this sutra are likewise so."
Ānanda! Those sentient beings who understand this sutra will stride like a lion, advancing toward the supreme path. Ānanda!
Future bodhisattvas will be able to take delight in this sutra. Ānanda!
This sutra can cause bodhisattvas to be courageous; after I have passed away, future bodhisattvas shall receive this sutra with their own hands and write it down with their own hands.

The seat for this sutra is not held in the hands of a *caṇḍāla* bodhisattva, nor is it obtained by the hands of a bodhisattva of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*), nor is it obtained by the hands of a bodhisattva of mere nominal designation (*prajñapti*).
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested himself in the likeness of Mañjuśrī.
Having assumed this form, Mañjuśrī also understood it thus:
"I shall now inquire of the World-Honored One regarding the profound Dharma, which is not the domain of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but is the stage of the bodhisattvas."
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to ask the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha a few questions; if the Buddha grants me permission, I shall venture to inquire.”
After Mañjuśrī had thus made his request, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
“Ask whatever you wish, according to your inclination; the entire assembly is gathered.”
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What is meant by a bodhisattva who is well able to abide securely in all dharmas of merit, manifesting all bodhisattva practices, teaching and transforming immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings, and appearing in the forms of Buddhas like the reflection of the moon in water?”
After Mañjuśrī had asked this, the Buddha immediately praised him,
saying: "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!"
"You have been able to ask the Tathāgata about this matter in brief; I shall now explain it to you in detail.
Mañjuśrī, listen closely, listen closely!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall now speak!
Mañjuśrī replied, "I shall receive these instructions and listen accordingly!"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“A bodhisattva who accomplishes six dharmas will attain and fully abide in all dharmas of merit.
What are these six?
Mañjuśrī! This bodhisattva’s giving is able to relinquish everything, yet he does not perceive a self that is free from the defilement of stinginess;
he dwells securely in ethical discipline, yet he does not perceive a "I" that is free from the karma of breaking precepts.
They achieve patience, yet do not perceive a self that can abandon the practice of anger;
they possess diligence, yet it is not a diligence of body or mind;
they know how to enter all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and skillful means, yet they do not conceive of themselves as achieving single-minded concentration.
There is the practice of wisdom, through which one clearly understands and personally realizes liberation from all paths. Mañjuśrī!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these six dharmas, they are well able to abide securely in all meritorious qualities.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, there are another six dharmas that are well able to establish all merits.
What are these six?
Mañjuśrī! These bodhisattvas, while dwelling within the hells, gather in sentient beings so that they may experience celestial bliss;
taking birth in the bodies of animals, they gather in animals so that they may receive sublime human pleasures.
Born into lowly families, they experience the bliss of a universal monarch;
manifesting entry into all realms of existence, they experience the bliss of the supreme path;
they skillfully know how to travel to and from all Buddha-fields, like the reflection of the moon in water.
They produce all speech, yet there is nothing spoken, and each remains unattached.
Mañjuśrī! A bodhisattva who accomplishes these six dharmas is able to abide securely in all meritorious qualities.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how is it that a bodhisattva, while dwelling in the hells, experiences celestial bliss?”
Having asked this question, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If a bodhisattva enters the samādhi called 'Great Lotus' and dwells within the hells, they gather in sentient beings and cause them to experience celestial bliss."

Seeing all sentient beings undergoing various kinds of suffering, he manifests his form before each of them and preaches the Dharma for them, causing immeasurable sentient beings to attain complete liberation. Mañjuśrī!
"In this way, the bodhisattva dwells within the hells while experiencing celestial bliss.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"How is it that a bodhisattva is born among animals, yet gathers in other animals and experiences the sublime bliss of humans and devas?"
The Buddha said, “Mañjuśrī!

This bodhisattva enters a samādhi called ‘Quiescence. Although he manifests birth among animals, he does not lose his mind; he experiences the sublime joys of gods and humans, preaching the Dharma for each according to their respective forms.”
The Bodhisattva establishes immeasurable thousands of beings in peace and causes them to abide in the Dharma. Mañjuśrī!
In this way, the Bodhisattva accepts birth in the bodies of animals, yet experiences the sublime joys of humans.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva is born into a lowly family yet experiences the pleasures of a wheel-turning monarch?”
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī! This bodhisattva has entered a samādhi called 'Tranquil Transcendence' (Śāntātikrama)."
By the power of this samādhi, one is born into a lowly family yet experiences the bliss of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Mañjuśrī! In this way, a bodhisattva is born into a lowly family and experiences the bliss of a universal monarch.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva manifest entry into the various paths while experiencing the bliss of the supreme path?”
The Buddha said,
“Mañjuśrī! This bodhisattva has entered a samādhi called ‘The Light of Seeing All Formations as Unconditioned.’”
When a bodhisattva abides in this samādhi, they manifest entry into all paths and experience the supreme bliss of the path.
Mañjuśrī! In this way, the bodhisattva manifests entry into all paths and experiences the supreme bliss of the path.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

How is it that a bodhisattva skillfully knows how to travel to and from all buddha-fields, yet remains unmoved from his original place and has neither coming nor going, manifesting all buddha-fields like the reflection of the moon in water?"
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī! This bodhisattva enters a samādhi called 'Transcending All Verbal Expression.'"

When this bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi, they manifest their body throughout all worlds in the ten directions—east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below—without moving from their original location and without coming or going;
dwelling in this samādhi, they are able to see all Buddhas and hear them preaching the Dharma.

Mañjuśrī! In this way, a bodhisattva skillfully knows how to travel to and from all buddha-fields; yet, without moving from their original place and without coming or going, they manifest all buddha-fields like the reflection of the moon in water.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva produces all speech while having nothing to say, such that each does not engage with the other?”
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī! This bodhisattva has attained a dhāraṇī called 'Immeasurable.'"
Having attained this retention, they enter immeasurable states of mind and understand immeasurable languages.
Because these bodhisattvas have attained the power of the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*, they produce all languages, each of which remains distinct and unmixed.
“Mañjuśrī! In this way, the bodhisattva produces all speech, yet there is nothing spoken, and each [utterance] is not approached as a substantial entity.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The skillful means of this bodhisattva are exceedingly difficult.
World-Honored One!”
"If there is a bodhisattva who enters this sutra, into what kind of dharma do they enter?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!..."
"If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to enter this sutra, it is like understanding empty space.
Mañjuśrī asked, "What is empty space?"
The Buddha said,
“Mañjuśrī! This space is not stained by desire, nor is it subject to anger or delusion.”
Mañjuśrī! All dharmas are likewise thus: they are without passion, hatred, or delusion. Mañjuśrī!
This space is not accomplished through generosity, nor through ethical discipline, nor through patience, nor through diligence, nor through meditative concentration, nor through wisdom.
In this way, Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are likewise:
they are not accomplished through giving, nor are they accomplished through morality, patience, diligence, meditation, or wisdom.
Mañjuśrī! Just as space is neither wisdom nor cessation. Mañjuśrī!
All dharmas are likewise thus: they are neither wisdom nor abandonment.
Mañjuśrī! Just as space is neither cultivated nor realized.
Mañjuśrī! All dharmas are likewise; they are neither cultivated nor realized. Mañjuśrī!
Just as space is neither dark nor light,
Mañjuśrī, so too are all phenomena: they are neither dark nor light.
Mañjuśrī! Just as space pervades all places yet cannot be grasped; Mañjuśrī!
All phenomena are likewise thus: they pervade all places yet cannot be grasped. Mañjuśrī!
Just as space neither proceeds upon the right path nor proceeds upon the wrong path.
Mañjuśrī! All dharmas are likewise thus: they do not advance upon the right path, nor do they advance upon the wrong path. Mañjuśrī!
Just as space is not the vehicle of the śrāvakas, nor the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, nor the vehicle of the buddhas;
Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are likewise: they are not the vehicle of the śrāvakas, nor the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, nor the vehicle of the buddhas.
Mañjuśrī! Just as space is neither thought nor wisdom. Mañjuśrī!
All dharmas are likewise thus: they are neither thought nor wisdom.
Mañjuśrī! Just as space is neither moving nor originating, yet neither non-moving nor non-originating.
Mañjuśrī! All dharmas are likewise thus: they neither move nor do they not move. Mañjuśrī!
Just as space is neither in motion nor not in motion,
Mañjuśrī, so too is the bodhisattva: with respect to all phenomena, they are neither in motion nor not in motion.
Mañjuśrī! Just as there is no sentient being capable of polluting space, Mañjuśrī!
All dharmas are likewise thus: they are portions of nirvāṇa, ultimately undefiled, neither quiescent nor non-quiescent. Mañjuśrī!
Just as space dwells in no dwelling place— remaining unmoving and unshakable because it has no abode—
so too, Mañjuśrī, are all bodhisattvas:
they see all sentient beings dwelling in no dwelling place, thereby attaining true immovability, unshakability, and non-abiding.
Mañjuśrī! This dharma of true reality—desiring to see the Tathāgata therein is called a false view;
such a false view is itself right practice.
If it were right practice, there would be no great fruit in giving within it, nor would there be a great reward;
if there were no great fruit or reward in that giving, it would be a field of merit for the world;
if it were a field of merit for the world, then the giving within it would have no fruit or reward.
If giving were without fruit and retribution, this would mean that the wisdom of unreality is fulfilled;
if that wisdom of unreality is fulfilled, such persons will swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
At that time, sixty monks within the assembly who were possessed of overweening pride, having heard such a teaching, thought to themselves: "This Way is obscure;
as the Tathāgata has taught it, it is identical to the teachings of the non-Buddhists."

The non-Buddhists such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarin Gośālīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra have taught in this way, and the Buddha has likewise taught in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of these sixty bhikṣus of overweening pride, addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!
"It is so, it is so! The Dharma taught by me, the Tathāgata, is identical to that of the non-Buddhists; yet those non-Buddhists do not understand the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.

At that time, sixty bhikṣus of overweening pride, having heard this statement, felt their suffering increase; they were distressed and displeased, their hearts were unhappy because they did not understand the Dharma thus taught, and they rose from their seats and departed.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked the bhikṣus:
"Venerable ones,
where do you intend to go now?"
One should understand for what cause and for what condition the Tathāgata taught the Dharma in this way; why did the Tathāgata speak thus at that time?
Venerable sir, please wait!
I shall ask the Tathāgata by what causes and conditions he spoke in this manner.
At that time, having heard the words of the Venerable Śāriputra, the bhikṣus immediately returned to their respective original seats.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what reason has the Tathāgata spoken of such matters? I pray that you will explain this to sever the doubts of the bhikṣus.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"What do you think? If there were bhikṣus whose outflows were already exhausted and whose minds had attained liberation, would those bhikṣus feel alarm or fear upon hearing these words?"
Śāriputra said:
“No, World-Honored One!

If there is a bhikṣu who has seen the Noble Truths, he will not be startled, terrified, or afraid upon hearing any sound; how much less so one whose outflows are exhausted and whose mind has attained liberation?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"There may be deluded people who, through false conceptualization and discrimination, attain the practice of emptiness regarding unreal dharmas.
Śāriputra said:
“May the World-Honored One explain the meaning of these Dharma verses so as to sever the doubts of the assembly!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“If one perceives the Tathāgata as being like a dream or like an illusion, this is called right view.”

If one possesses right view, one does not form the notion of reality regarding the Tathāgata, nor the notion of solidity, nor the notion of substance, nor the notion of name, nor the notion of a collection.

If one acts in such a way as not to form these notions of reality, solidity, substance, name, or collection regarding the Tathāgata, then all such conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are entirely false views.
If all conditioned formations are entirely false views, then one knows that all dharmas are wrong views.
If one knows that all dharmas are false views, the Buddha says that such [knowing] fulfills false views;
furthermore, to know that all views are false is itself a false view.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
For this reason, to wish to see the Tathāgata is called a false view. Śāriputra!
These people do not see the secret body of the Tathāgata; they grasp at conceptual distinctions, perceiving the body of the Tathāgata as being nothing other than the śarīras. Śāriputra!
"If one holds such a view regarding the Tathāgata, it is called false knowledge.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How can wrong view be called right practice?
The Buddha said,
"Śāriputra!..."

All ordinary beings, giving rise to applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), engage in false conceptualization and discrimination; they give rise to dependence, movement, and non-movement; they give rise to the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), the view of a sentient being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*), the view of a life-force (*jīva-dṛṣṭi*), and the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*); and they become attached to "I am superior" and "mine is superior."
Knowing these various matters, ordinary worldlings waver in their worldly affairs and give rise to conceptual proliferation; they know that all such things are entirely unreal. Śāriputra!
That which is non-existent is called unreal.
Śāriputra, that which is unreal is called false speech.
Śāriputra! One who speaks falsely is called "perverse. Śāriputra!
Such matters as these grasp what is unreal; these wrong views are called right practice.
Śāriputra! For this reason, what are called wrong views are termed right practice.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is there a right practice such that all acts of giving bear neither small nor great fruits?”
The Buddha said: “Śāriputra!
If one thus accomplishes such right practice, whatever they give will be directed toward nirvāṇa, will partake of nirvāṇa, and will be equal to nirvāṇa.”
Śāriputra! This nirvāṇa has neither small fruits nor great fruits, nor is it a matter of small merit. Why is this?
"This Nirvana is free from all fruits; it has no equal division, and it cannot be divided.
Śāriputra said, "World-Honored One!"
“If nirvāṇa has no limits, why does the Tathāgata speak of increasing immeasurable and boundless merit?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“Ordinary beings are possessed of afflictions—they hold theories of a self, theories of a sentient being, theories of a life-force, and theories of a person. For the sake of such beings as these, I say that nirvāṇa has no limits, and that nirvāṇa increases immeasurable merit, even to the point of causing them to give rise to a mind of joyful aspiration.”
Śāriputra! Even a provisional holy field of merit does not enter nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
“Śāriputra, those noble ones who have abandoned desire are called ‘fields of merit.
It is, for example, like a farmer who sows grain seeds; while the grain grows, weeds and other grasses also grow along with it.”
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Is this weed obtained by that farmer a karmic retribution?
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra, it is like a farmer who, depending on grain seeds, produces weeds such as barnyard grass, yet also produces grain that resembles [the original seed].”
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
Giving to the holy field of merit brings about a natural and great retribution; subsequently, one severs all outflows and dries up the fruit of craving. Śāriputra!
However, this farmer’s original intention was for grain; seeing the other weeds, he felt no joy in his heart, because they were not the fruit [he sought] and were not beneficial.
In the same way, Śāriputra!
It is not a field of merit; one who bestows gifts upon such a person, though they may be a noble one, will not obtain a great fruit or reward.
Śāriputra, for this reason, giving to one who practices correctly does not result in a great fruit or great reward.
Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!
If giving results in neither great fruit nor great retribution, why is it called the World’s Field of Merit?”
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra, it is not through the notion of a small fruit, nor through the notion of a great fruit, that this giving arises."
If giving does not arise, one is able to receive the offerings of the world’s devas,
humans, and asuras. Śāriputra,
in the field of the inexhaustible, one neither takes up nor bestows karmic retribution.
"Therefore, Śāriputra,
it is neither a great recompense nor a small fruit that constitutes a field of merit for the world.
Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that this field of merit for the world does not yield fruit and retribution?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"What do you think? Is there any karmic retribution for [the pursuit of] nirvāṇa?
Śāriputra replied, "No, World-Honored One."
“If giving were to result in the attainment of karmic retribution for the sake of nirvana, then all noble ones would not be called unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
The Buddha then praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"Śāriputra! For this reason, giving to those who are not fields of merit for the world yields no karmic fruit.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If giving has no retribution, how can one be fully endowed with the wisdom of conceptualization?
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Is it true that one knows the nature of all phenomena to be real?
Śāriputra replied:
“World-Honored One!
[I] know that all dharmas are like the nature of an illusion.
World-Honored One!”
If one knows that the nature of illusion is unreal, why is this?
Because the Tathāgata has taught that all phenomena are like the nature of illusion.
That which has the nature of an illusion is, indeed, unreal.
World-Honored One!
If one knows that the nature of all phenomena is thus, this is the wisdom of unreality.
"Why is this? Because there is not a single dharma that is real.
At that time, the Buddha again praised Śāriputra:
“Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra! So it is, so it is!”
Śāriputra! If dharmas possessed substantiality, material existence, or reality, then no sentient beings would enter nirvāṇa. Śāriputra!
All dharmas are likewise not real; they are neither substantial entities nor true.

Therefore, Śāriputra, although as many sentient beings as there are sands in the Ganges enter nirvāṇa and never again take birth, one does not perceive their exhaustion, because sentient beings are not real.
Śāriputra! If all sentient beings have no notion of reality, this is called being fully endowed with the wisdom of non-reality.
Therefore, Śāriputra!
"Giving has no karmic fruit; one can thereby attain the fulfillment of the wisdom of unreality.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that one whose wisdom is perfected, regarding what is unreal wisdom, swiftly attains the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena?
The Buddha said,
"Śāriputra!..."
If one knows it is unreal yet does not realize it—
Śāriputra, what is that which is unreal?
The view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-force, the view of a person, the view of annihilationism, and the view of eternalism.
Furthermore, there are unreal notions: the notion of a Buddha, the notion of the Dharma, the notion of the Saṅgha, and the notion of nirvāṇa.
Śāriputra! If the mind wavers, all conceptual proliferation and worldly activities are entirely unreal. Śāriputra!
In this way, one attains liberation within that which is unreal. Śāriputra!
By means of this matter, one possesses the wisdom of unreality and swiftly attains the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena.

When this Dharma was being taught, forty-two thousand people attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); sixty thousand upāsakas resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; and thirty-six thousand devaputras attained the realization of wisdom.
These sixty bhikṣus of overweening pride severed all outflows, and their minds attained liberation.
Once their minds were liberated, they spoke these words with one voice:
“World-Honored One!
I have only now left the six teachers to go forth.
From this day forward, the Buddha is not my honored one; nor shall I mind the Dharma, nor shall I mind the Sangha.
World-Honored One!
"From this day forward, I shall preach non-action, preach the absence of causal conditions, preach the absence of karma, and preach the absence of discipline.
At that time, various beings within the assembly each spoke these words: "These bhikṣus!"
"Or they may abandon the Buddha's precepts, don the robes of non-Buddhists, and speak with inverted views.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, perceiving the thoughts of the assembly, spoke to the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable ones!..."
"For what reason did you speak these words: 'I have only now begun my renunciation under the six teachers'?
The bhikṣus said, "Venerable Śāriputra!"
From this day forward, the six teachers and all other masters shall be of one and the same nature, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Venerable Śāriputra!
We now know that these teachers are not different; because there is no discrimination within the state of leaving home, we speak of "leaving home."
Śāriputra said, “Virtuous One!
For what reason do you say, ‘From now on, the Buddha is no longer my honored teacher’?”
The bhikṣus said:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
From this day forward, we shall naturally be clear-sighted, blazing with brilliance, and no longer dependent on any other light."
I take refuge in myself and not in anything else; I honor myself and thus say, "The Buddha is not my honored one. Why is this?
"I am not separate from the Buddha, and the Buddha is not separate from me.
Śāriputra said,
"Virtuous One!"
"For what reason do you say such things as, 'One does not bring the Dharma to mind,
nor does one bring the Saṅgha to mind'? The bhikṣus said, "Venerable Śāriputra!"
From this day forward, I shall not find any dharma to be grasped, whether by mindfulness or by concentration; therefore, I say: "From this day forth, I shall not dwell upon the Sangha."
Śāriputra said: "Virtuous One!
Why do you say, 'From this day forward, I shall speak of non-action'?"
The bhikṣus said:
"Venerable Śāriputra!

From this day forward, we shall know that all dharmas are unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*); herein there is neither action nor non-action. For this reason, we say: 'From this day forth, we speak of the unconditioned.'"
Śāriputra said: "Venerable sir, for what reason do you say,
'From now on, I shall speak of the absence of causes and conditions'?"
The bhikṣus said:
"Venerable Śāriputra!

From this day forth, for us all, the causes and conditions for the arising of the path have been exhausted; herein there is no cause. For this reason, we say: 'From now on, I declare that there is neither cause nor condition.'"
Śāriputra said: "Virtuous One!
For what reason do you say, 'From this day forward, I shall speak of the non-existence of karma'?"
The bhikṣus said:
“Venerable Śāriputra!
From this day forward, we know that all dharmas are ultimately nirvāṇa; therein is neither discipline nor non-discipline. For this reason, I say, ‘I teach that there is no karma.’”
When those bhikṣus of overweening pride spoke this Dharma, three thousand six hundred bhikṣus completely severed all outflows, and their minds attained liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the bhikṣus:
“Excellent, excellent!
Within this true aspiration, not a single dharma can be apprehended.”
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
regarding what is called ‘attainment,’ what dharma is named attainment?”
The Buddha said:
"Mañjuśrī! That which is attained is called the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)."
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One,
how should a bodhisattva who wishes to attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) train?”
How does one practice?
How does one abide?
How does one cultivate and accumulate?

At that time, in response to the question posed by the youth Mañjuśrī regarding the meaning of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If there are those who seek the Buddha-wisdom, The supreme among all forms of wisdom, There is no dharma to be grasped, Nor is there any dharma to be abandoned."
There is no dharma that can be apprehended.
If birth were an existent thing, there would be no compounded phenomena, yet ordinary beings desire such compounding.
That which can be known and severed—the Dharma taught for the sake of sentient beings—[is likewise empty].
Ordinary beings give rise to conditioned phenomena and do not believe in the dharma of non-arising.
They abandon the dharmas of Māra; the path to Bodhi is supreme.
Ordinary beings are attached to dualistic dharmas and do not know the non-dual dharma.
Various illusions have no reality; ordinary people perceive them as distinct, yet within them there is no distinction—they are all of one single characteristic.
If an ordinary person were to say:
"Non-dual and without the act of making non-dual, all are equal like illusions.
Ordinary people may say:
"I shall at some time exhaust desire, sever hatred and delusion,"
I shall contemplate well:
reckoning cessation as nirvana, I will destroy greed, hatred, and delusion,
and teach the Dharma of emptiness.
This is called Nirvana; for those who exert themselves to give rise to [such] progress, they are far removed from my Dharma.
Those who take pleasure in the notion of Bodhi do not enter into Bodhi.
Those who practice by means of conceptualizing thoughts do not understand that all phenomena are empty; though all phenomena are of one single mark,
they should each be explained differently.
Their essential nature is without difference; just as five fingers are called a "hand," attaining bodhi is not difficult.
There is no one who approaches bodhi, nor is there anyone distinct from it or separate from it.
They are far removed from awakening;
each regards the other as wrong, saying, "This one has perfected the precepts," while "that one is evil for breaking them."
All conditioned phenomena lack reality; wisdom does not grasp them as solid, knowing them to be like illusions and transformations.
Even the breaking of precepts lacks reality; all dharmas arise from causes and conditions.
In this there is no self;
though I give alms to recipients and uphold the unsurpassed precepts,
the Buddhas do not bestow a prediction upon me.
When the perception of giving was left without remainder and all inversions were abandoned, at that time I received the prediction.
By upholding pure precepts one is born in heaven; herein there is nothing to be attained.
This is unsurpassed bodhi.
Through the deluded recollections of ignorance, we have attained patience,
which is unconditioned and without arising.
For one who does not conceptualize birth, it is not difficult to attain this patience throughout billions of kalpas.
Phenomena have no creator; they have no fundamental place of abiding.
All are like the appearance of empty space;
because greed, hatred, and delusion have been severed, he expounds the unsurpassed Dharma,
a Dharma that can never be exhausted.
Swiftly they return to exhaustion; such unreal phenomena are the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), which cannot be grasped.
Ignorance is likewise boundless; if one does not perceive reality, [how can it be attained]?
Nor can it be found within the middle.
Since there is no sprout within the seed, where could the fruit and leaves be?
If the leaves cannot be found, the flower likewise cannot be found.
Sentient beings shall give birth to children; yet they neither arise nor emerge—this is seeing things as they truly are.
In the end, there are no children at all, for because there are no children, [there is no birth].
Nor is there any anxiety for one's children.
Since all phenomena are unarisen, there is no fear of undergoing the suffering of birth and death.
Not knowing that dharmas are like illusions, one bears the heavy burden of empty space;
this is the delusion of those lacking wisdom.
Without reality and without limit, they are immeasurable and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya).
In this there is no delusion;
I call this the "limitless. The future limit is likewise so;
the limit of sentient beings is inconceivable—the limitless is the limit of conceptualization.
Space has no limits; because one understands this meaning, one’s wisdom is non-dual.
The limit of sentient beings is inconceivable; the primordial limit is like a reflection in a mirror.
This wisdom has nothing to be known.
One who practices such discrimination thinks in their mind:
"When shall I exhaust all evil?"
"When shall I become a Buddha?
Within this there is no conjunction; dharmas have no conjoiner, yet ordinary beings desire conjunction."
Nor does it have a place of abiding; because space has no abode, it is unimpeded and devoid of substance.
Thus is space described; thus should one know bodhi.
Knowing awakening in this way, one knows sentient beings in the same manner.
Since the realm of sentient beings is equal, if one knows such equality,
attaining awakening is not difficult.
Without conceptualizing or performing virtuous deeds, and with nothing coming forth within the Dharma,
awakening is not difficult to attain.
Having severed all seeking, there is no mind that can grasp it.
Awakening to unsurpassed bodhi:
through giving one attains bodhi, yet ultimately one does not attain bodhi;
one cannot achieve bodhi.
To conceive of diligence as real is not the sublime diligence of the Buddha's Dharma;
such is the conceptualization of recollection.
It is not that I am not free from inversion, for from the very beginning there has been no stirring or arising.
This goodness is unsurpassed;
this dharma is without outflows (anāsrava), while this dharma has outflows (sāsrava)—
such a person’s mind is not good.
This is identical to space, neither bound nor liberated;
this wisdom is unsurpassed.
To conceive of these as "evil transgressions of the precepts" is itself to break both sets of precepts.
The unsurpassed precepts are non-dual;
the precepts have no characteristics of increase or decrease. Those who perceive this nature are the ones who protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
Just like a bird in the sky, Knowing thus in full measure is the true Dharma of a śramaṇa.
Not conceptualizing anything at all, Without mind, without self, and without life-principle.
Attaining bodhi is not difficult.
Not being led astray by desire, yet not abandoning lustful desire—
this is how bodhi is not difficult.
"At the limit of fearlessness, there is no alarm or dread regarding birth and death;
thus, awakening is not difficult to attain.
When the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:

“Mañjuśrī! If there is a bodhisattva who believes and understands this sutra without doubt or hesitation, who receives, maintains, reads, and recites it until they have mastered it, and who explains it extensively for others, that person shall obtain twenty merits.”
What are these twenty?
The devas shall protect them;
the nāgas shall protect them;
They are protected by yakṣas;
their minds are always free from distraction;
and at the end of life, they recognize their own past lives in the place where they are reborn.
At the end of life, wherever they are reborn, they shall attain the five supernormal powers;
at the end of life, wherever they are reborn, they shall behold Maitreya Bodhisattva;
and they shall maintain mindfulness of this sūtra and its Dharma without their minds becoming distracted, except during sleep or within dreams.
One who sees the Buddha also sees the Bodhisattvas;
those who believe and understand this sutra attain the Patience of Accordance;
those who keep this sutra in mind sever anger in the present life.
Those who uphold this sutra shall attain fearlessness even when amidst venomous snakes;
those who recollect this sutra shall subdue evil elephants;
those who recollect this sutra shall attain the Samādhi of Universal Illumination.
Those who study this sutra will exhaust all karmic obstacles of evil;
when they preach this sutra, they will attain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates, thereby never losing the bodhicitta and attaining the immeasurable *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*.
Those who keep this sutra in mind will never find any demonic activities able to arise.
They shall also be born before the Buddhas of the present and attain all auspicious and virtuous vows.
Those who recite this sutra will receive protection among all venomous creatures—whether footless, two-footed, three-footed, or four-footed.
Those who recite this sutra will have no fear of non-human beings and shall be protected from the wrath of kings.
Mañjuśrī! These are the twenty merits of a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma,
because he upholds this sutra with a mind free from doubt, recites it until he has mastered it, and explains it extensively for others.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
They are like various medicinal trees that eliminate all illnesses.”
“World-Honored One!
This sutra is also like this; it cuts off all illnesses.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! Mañjuśrī, you have spoken these words well."
This sutra can sever all illnesses. Why is this? Mañjuśrī!

In the past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, and again beyond another incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there was a Buddha named Siṃhavikrāntagāmin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who appeared in the world and expounded this sutra before an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands.
Mañjuśrī! At that time, there was a bodhisattva among the assembly named Vajradhvaja.

Having heard this Dharma of the sutra from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, his mind was free from doubt. Because he had received and upheld this Sūtra of Sublime Merit, and because he had mastered it, understood it, entered into it, and attained its power, he proclaimed it himself in villages, towns, and royal palaces, saying:
"I am a skilled physician.
At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, oppressed by various illnesses, all came to the place where this Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva was.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, with a heart of loving-kindness and skillful understanding, used the dharani verses of this sutra-dharma to gather in, protect, and sustain all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī! What are these dhāraṇī phrases?

“Āraṇe 1, pācale 2, vinine 3, sūtata 4, sūpeta 5, anucche 6, vipannahe 7, khagaluha 8, mayisugge 9, anujajjate 10, nalaite 11, milāsumilā 12, suraheḍe 13, sarvatāre 14, ṅgakaṅga 15, hyayohā 16, macumacihā 17. By means of these dhāraṇī phrases, one shall protect and gather in those sentient beings, removing various diseases—whether from being bitten by venomous snakes, leprosy, or wind-disorders.
Mañjuśrī! This Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja uses this Dharma of the sutra to settle sentient beings and eliminate all their ailments. Mañjuśrī!
Do you think that the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja at that time was someone else?
Do not view it thus! Why is this?
"I was the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja at that time; by explaining this sutra, I have brought great benefit to sentient beings.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"If a bodhisattva receives and maintains these dhāraṇī verses, reciting them until they are mastered, what is it appropriate for them to practice, and what dharma rules should they follow?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!..."

If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to penetrate the phrases and chapters of this dhāraṇī, they should practice pure conduct: not eat meat, not anoint their feet with oil, and not frequent large crowds. They should always give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward sentient beings; they must not read this sutra as one who is unrighteous or impure, nor should they read it in an impure place.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a bodhisattva who reads this sutra, they will not spare their own body or life.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is! Mañjuśrī!"
"It is as you have said.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda: "Ānanda!"
"You should receive and uphold this sutra; this sutra shall, in the future, bring great benefit to sentient beings.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"As the Buddha has taught, I have already received and upheld it.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Ānanda! In a future age, you shall become a venerable guide for the multitude.
At that time, sentient beings who read and recite this sutra shall do so as if receiving it directly from me.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, the Venerable Śāriputra, the youth Mañjuśrī, as well as the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly filled with joy.
The Sūtra on the Elephant’s Armpit Spoken by the Buddha
